The decoder stack adds a third sub‑layer that performs multi‑head attention over the encoder’s output, whereas the encoder stack contains only self‑attention and feed‑forward sub‑layers [AIAYN:3.1:c009].

In the decoder’s self‑attention sub‑layer positions are masked so that each position can attend only to earlier positions, preserving the auto‑regressive property, while the encoder’s self‑attention allows every position to attend to all positions in the previous encoder layer [AIAYN:3.2.3:c016].
In encoder‑decoder attention layers, the queries are taken from the previous decoder layer, and the keys and values are taken from the output of the encoder [AIAYN:3.2.3:c016].
The decoder therefore differs by incorporating masked self‑attention and an additional cross‑attention sub‑layer that draws its queries from the decoder and its keys/values from the encoder.
The decoder stack includes a third sub‑layer that performs multi‑head attention over the encoder output, while the encoder stack does not have this layer [AIAYN:3.1:c009].
In encoder self‑attention all queries, keys and values come from the same previous encoder layer [AIAYN:3.2.3:c016].
In decoder self‑attention each position can attend only to positions up to and including that position, using masking to prevent leftward information flow [AIAYN:3.2.3:c016].
Encoder‑decoder attention uses queries from the previous decoder layer and keys and values from the encoder output [AIAYN:3.2.3:c016].

The authors chose sinusoidal positional encodings because they hypothesized that the sinusoid functions would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PE_{pos+k} can be represented as a linear function of PE_{pos} [AIAYN:3.5:c020].
They also noted that the sinusoidal version may enable extrapolation to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training [AIAYN:3.5:c020].

When they tried learned positional embeddings instead, they observed nearly identical results to the base model, with a dev perplexity of 4.92 and BLEU of 25.7, indicating no significant performance difference [AIAYN:T3:r08][AIAYN:6.2:c031].

The authors used sine and cosine functions of different frequencies for positional encodings because they hypothesized that this would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PE_{pos+k} can be represented as a linear function of PE_{pos} [AIAYN:3.5:c020].
They also chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those encountered during training [AIAYN:3.5:c020].
They experimented with learned positional embeddings instead and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results [AIAYN:3.5:c020].

In Table 3 row (E) they replaced sinusoidal positional encoding with learned positional embeddings and observed a dev perplexity of 4.92 and BLEU of 25.7, essentially matching the base model [AIAYN:T3:r08][AIAYN:6.2:c031].
